newsitem.title: USA: Clinton may name more U.S. Supreme Court justices.
newsitem.headline: Clinton may name more U.S. Supreme Court justices.

text.p: President Clinton in the next four years may get several coveted Supreme Court appointments, bolstering the influence of moderate justices and leaving behind a judicial legacy, legal experts said Wednesday.

They said Clinton, fresh from a re-election victory but still facing a Republican-controlled Senate, most likely would name judges similar to his first two appointees -- Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer -- to any vacancies.

They agreed that Clinton probably would not be known for reshaping the nine-member high court, splintered among conservative, moderate and liberal factions. Instead, he probably would be best remembered for helping stop the court's dramatic shift to the right, especially on contentious social issues such as abortion rights and church-state separation.

"Clinton's Supreme Court legacy will parallel the place he found himself politically during the past two years. An instinct for the middle ground will have prevailed," said University of Virginia law professor A.E. Dick Howard.
He predicted that future Clinton appointees would be modelled after Ginsburg and Breyer, "solid, seasoned and uncontroversial figures who are talented and experienced."
None of the current Supreme Court members, who have lifetime tenure, has announced plans to leave the bench. But the experts said as many as three could retire before 2000, depending on their health.
The most likely would be Justice John Paul Stevens, the court's most liberal and oldest member at 75, who was appointed to the court by President Gerald Ford in 1975.

The other two possibilities are Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, 66, and Chief Justice William Rehnquist, 72, both appointed by Republican presidents, but the experts cautioned they may decide to stay until the next presidential election.

If Rehnquist does step down, Clinton may elevate Ginsburg to his post, making her the first woman to serve as chief justice, Sheldon Goldman, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts in Amherst, said.

The experts said a leading candidate for any vacancy would be Jose Cabranes, who would be the first Hispanic-American on the court. Originally named a federal judge, Cabranes was elevated to the U.S. appeals court in Connecticut by Clinton.

Goldman also said Clinton may decide to name a more liberal black justice to counter the influence of Justice Clarence Thomas, a staunch conservative and the second black to sit on the court. A leading contender would be Drew Days, a former U.S. solicitor general under Clinton who returned in June to Yale University as a law professor.
University of Chicago law professor Cass Sunstein said he expected Clinton to pick "non-ideological, first-rate" appointees who were carefully chosen to avoid a bruising Senate confirmation battle.

A Justice Department official said Clinton would review the same lists used during the last two vacancies. Among those likely to get renewed consideration were Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger and U.S. appeals court judge Richard Arnold from Arkansas.
